planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed overwinters in place and cold-stratifies naturally in the leaf litter; this rare Appalachian mint is notoriously slow to establish from purchased seed and does best sown fresh into undisturbed woodland soil rather than started indoors.

directions: Sow or transplant into deep, moist, calcium-rich woodland soil in full to dappled shade, mimicking the limestone cove forests and rich streamside slopes of the central Appalachians where this uncommon biennial-to-short-lived-perennial mint naturalizes. In its second spring it sends up soft, hairy stems topped with tubular, pale cream-to-white flowers heavily veined and blotched in purple, resembling a small foxglove and blooming for several weeks in April and May before most other woodland flowers have finished. Because populations are scattered and easily overlooked, source seed or plants only from reputable native nurseries rather than wild-collecting. Once content, it self-sows modestly along shaded seeps and rich slopes but rarely becomes aggressive, making it a good choice for restoring diversity to an established woodland garden.

planting.note: Divide creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new shoots emerge and set them into consistently moist, humus-rich shade soil; this diminutive forest-floor spreader establishes quickly from divisions and fills in bare patches under trees within a season or two.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, where this native eastern woodland groundcover forms low colonies of soft, heart-shaped leaves topped in mid-to-late summer by wiry, airy racemes of tiny two-petaled white flowers. The flowers are followed by small bristly burs that cling readily to fur and clothing, the plant's main means of dispersal, so site it away from paths where the burs will be a nuisance. It is a modest but useful filler for the deepest, driest shade under mature trees where few other natives will thrive, spreading gently by rhizome without becoming a nuisance in most garden settings. Its unassuming, almost fern-like texture makes an excellent low backdrop for showier spring ephemerals that have already gone dormant by the time it blooms.

planting.note: Divide tuberous roots or transplant nursery-grown crowns in fall into rich, consistently moist woodland soil; fresh seed sown outdoors in autumn needs a full winter of cold, moist stratification and often takes a second winter to germinate, so division is the far more reliable way to establish this species in a garden setting.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade along streambanks and forest edges, conditions that mimic the wet Appalachian coves and seepage slopes this scrambling native vine-like perennial calls home. Unlike the stiff, upright hybrid monkshoods common in cottage gardens, southern monkshood has a lax, sprawling habit and benefits from the light support of neighboring shrubs or a small trellis to display its hooded, deep violet-blue flowers, which appear in loose clusters from late summer into fall when few other woodland natives are still blooming. All parts of the plant are highly toxic if ingested and can irritate skin on contact, so gloves are recommended when handling roots or foliage and it should be sited away from children's play areas. Once established in favorable conditions it is long-lived and slowly forms an expanding patch, providing valuable late-season nectar for bumblebees strong enough to force open its distinctive hooded blooms.

planting.note: Transplant divisions in fall into cool, moist, acidic woodland soil under conifers or mixed hardwoods; this small violet resents heat and summer drought, so establish it in permanently shaded, humus-rich ground where it won't dry out between rains.

directions: Plant in cool, consistently moist, acidic soil in deep shade beneath hemlocks or northern hardwoods, the cool understory this diminutive violet prefers across its range from New England south along the Appalachians. Its nearly round, low-lying leaves lie flat against the forest floor and lengthen noticeably by summer, while small, bright yellow flowers with faint purple-brown veining on the lower petals appear close to the ground in early spring. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form a tight, ground-hugging mat rather than running aggressively, making it a well-behaved choice for a shaded rock garden or the base of a woodland planting. Because it struggles in heat and dry soil, it is best suited to northern gardens or cooler mountain microclimates rather than the lowland South.

planting.note: Divide rosettes in fall and set into dry-to-average, well-drained woodland soil in shade; this violet tolerates drier duff than most native violets, so avoid overly rich, wet planting spots that favor more aggressive violet species instead.

directions: Plant in dry-to-average, well-drained soil in full to partial shade beneath oak-hickory canopy, where this compact southeastern violet is often found carpeting dry ridges and upland woods that stay too dry for most other native violets. Its velvety, gray-green leaves are marked with a distinctive purple-silver sheen along the veins, an attractive foliage feature that persists well after the small violet-blue flowers finish in early spring. It stays neatly clumped rather than spreading by stolons, so it makes a tidy, low-maintenance groundcover for a shaded rock garden or the dry, root-filled ground beneath mature deciduous trees. Combine it with other dry-shade natives to build a low-care woodland edge planting in the difficult ground under established shade trees.

planting.note: Transplant divisions in fall into rich, moist, well-drained slopes in shade; give this southern Appalachian violet a woodland setting with dappled light and leaf-mold-enriched soil rather than deep, dense shade for the best foliage display and bloom.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil on shaded slopes and coves in the southern Appalachians and adjacent uplands, where this distinctive violet produces variable foliage ranging from simple heart-shaped leaves to deeply three-parted, almost fern-like leaves on the same plant. Bright yellow flowers with dark purple-brown lower-petal veining open in early spring just above the emerging foliage, then give way to the plant's ornamental, dissected summer leaves that persist as an attractive groundcover long after bloom. It forms slowly spreading clumps rather than running stolons, staying well-mannered in a shaded rock garden or along a woodland path edge. Its unusual leaf variability makes it a conversation piece among native-plant collectors and a worthwhile addition to a diverse woodland violet collection.
